newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-Pay tax break seen as victim of UK budget.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Pay tax break seen as victim of UK budget.

text.p: Tax relief on profit-related pay (PRP) is expected to be a casualty of the British budget to be delivered by Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke on November 26, a Reuters survey of economists showed.
In a survey of 27 economists asking their predictions for the budget, several said tax relief on PRP schemes was likely to be limited.

"If the chancellor were looking for a way to fund a larger personal income tax giveaway, whilst giving the overall impression of fiscal neutrality, then he may dip into PRP relief," said Alex Garrard, UK economist at UBS.
Profit-related pay links a portion of salaries to a company's performance, theoretically providing an incentive for a boosting of corporate profits.
Members of the British parliament's Treasury Select Committee have said they expect Clarke to clamp down on tax relief on profit-related pay.
But its complete abolition is unlikely, analysts say.
With an election due by May, the Conservative government would not want to risk alienating those who currently benefit the most from tax relief on PRP.
"Despite the persuasive economic case for its removal, the burden would fall on Conservative party supporters," said Garrard.
"Currently companies are simply using it as a tax break to enable them to award a government-subsidised pay rise. It is becoming an increasingly expensive tax break," he added.

PRP was introduced as a temporary measure in 1987 by former Chancellor Nigel Lawson, also a Conservative, who hoped to improve labour market flexibility by allowing wages to fluctuate with company profitability.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies, which has suggested for some years that PRP relief be phased out, estimates the cost of the scheme to be 1.5 billion sterling in the current financial year, compared with one billion in 1995/96.
The number of PRP schemes grew slowly from 615 in 1988 to 1,277 in 1991 and then mushroomed by 1996 to more than 12,000.
"The costs of PRP in future years are impossible to estimate. Its usage is exploding at an exponential rate," said Alissa Goodman, research economist at the IFS.
Analysts say the chancellor may opt to revert to the pre-1991 system, in which tax relief was only available on half of the profit-related payment.
Pay eligible for PRP relief was originally limited to 3,000 sterling but was raised in 1989 to 4,000.
Taxpayers currently paying the basic rate of 24 percent can save 960 sterling in a PRP scheme. At the higher rate of 40 percent, taxpayers stand to gain 1,600 sterling.
